1 Thessalonians 1: Paul, Silvanus, and Timothy write from Corinth about AD 50–51, a few months after founding the church at Thessalonica (Acts 17:1–9). It is probably one of Paul's earliest letters.
1 Thessalonians 2: Paul recalls his weeks in Thessalonica after being mistreated at Philippi.
1 Thessalonians 3: Paul had sent Timothy from Athens to Thessalonica; Timothy has now returned with good news (1 Thessalonians 3:1–6; Acts 18:5).
1 Thessalonians 4: Some members of the young church have died since Paul left, and the others grieve (1 Thessalonians 4:13).
1 Thessalonians 5: Paul ends by asking that the letter be read to all the believers (1 Thessalonians 5:27).
2 Thessalonians 1: Paul, Silvanus, and Timothy write again, probably from Corinth soon after the first letter, about AD 51. Some scholars think it was written later in Paul's name.
2 Thessalonians 2: Some in Thessalonica have heard that "the day of Christ is at hand" (2 Thessalonians 2:2), perhaps through a letter falsely claiming to be Paul's.
2 Thessalonians 3: Paul addresses members who refuse to work and signs the letter in his own hand (2 Thessalonians 3:17).
1 Timothy 1: Paul writes to Timothy, whom he left at Ephesus when he went to Macedonia (1 Timothy 1:3), probably in the early 60s AD, after the imprisonment of Acts 28. Many scholars think 1 and 2 Timothy and Titus were written later in Paul's name.
1 Timothy 2: Paul gives instructions for prayer "for kings, and for all that are in authority" (1 Timothy 2:2), under the emperor Nero.
1 Timothy 3: Paul lists qualifications for overseers and deacons in the Ephesian church.
1 Timothy 4: Paul warns of teachers forbidding marriage and certain foods.
1 Timothy 5: Paul gives instructions for supporting widows and honoring elders.
1 Timothy 6: Paul addresses slaves, false teachers, and the rich, and recalls Jesus' witness "before Pontius Pilate" (1 Timothy 6:13).
2 Timothy 1: Paul writes from prison in Rome (2 Timothy 1:8, 17), traditionally his last letter, shortly before his death under Nero, about AD 64–67.
2 Timothy 2: Paul is "bound" but says "the word of God is not bound" (2 Timothy 2:9).
2 Timothy 3: Paul recalls his sufferings at Antioch, Iconium, and Lystra (2 Timothy 3:11), Timothy's home region.
2 Timothy 4: Paul expects to die soon. Demas has left for Thessalonica and only Luke is with him; Timothy is to come before winter (2 Timothy 4:6–11, 21).
Titus 1: Paul writes to Titus, whom he left in Crete to appoint elders (Titus 1:5), probably in the early 60s AD. Crete had been a Roman province since 67 BC.
Titus 2: Paul tells Titus what to teach older men and women, younger men and women, and slaves in Crete's churches.
Titus 3: Paul plans to winter at Nicopolis, on the west coast of Greece, and asks Titus to join him there (Titus 3:12).
Philemon 1: Paul writes from prison, usually dated to Rome about AD 60–62, to Philemon of Colossae. Onesimus carries it along with the letter to the Colossians (Colossians 4:9).
Hebrews 1: Hebrews names no author or destination. Its readers know the Old Testament in Greek, and the greeting from "they of Italy" (Hebrews 13:24) suggests a link to Italy. Many date it before the temple's destruction in AD 70.
Hebrews 2: The writer and readers heard the message from those who heard the Lord (Hebrews 2:3), a second generation of believers.
Hebrews 3: The writer compares the readers with Israel in the wilderness, quoting Psalm 95.
Hebrews 4: The writer speaks of entering God's rest, drawing on Genesis 2:2 and Psalm 95.
Hebrews 5: The writer compares Jesus with Israel's high priests, chosen from among men.
Hebrews 6: The writer points to God's oath to Abraham (Genesis 22:16–17).
Hebrews 7: The writer discusses Melchisedec, king of Salem, who met Abraham (Genesis 14:18–20).
Hebrews 8: Priests still "offer gifts according to the law" (Hebrews 8:4), and the writer quotes Jeremiah 31:31–34.
Hebrews 9: The writer describes the tabernacle of Moses' time and the Day of Atonement.
Hebrews 10: The writer recalls the readers' early sufferings: public insults, prison, and loss of property (Hebrews 10:32–34).
Hebrews 11: The writer surveys people of faith from Abel through the prophets and later martyrs.
Hebrews 12: The readers "have not yet resisted unto blood" (Hebrews 12:4): none had yet been killed for their faith.
Hebrews 13: Timothy has been set free (Hebrews 13:23), and "they of Italy" send greetings.
James 1: James writes "to the twelve tribes which are scattered abroad" (James 1:1). Tradition identifies him as the brother of Jesus and leader of the Jerusalem church, who was stoned in AD 62 (Josephus).
James 2: James warns against favoring a rich man with a gold ring over a poor man in the assembly.
James 3: James warns teachers about the tongue.
James 4: James addresses merchants who plan a year's trading in a city (James 4:13).
James 5: James condemns rich landowners who keep back the wages of their field workers (James 5:4).
1 Peter 1: Peter writes to believers in Pontus, Galatia, Cappadocia, Asia, and Bithynia (1 Peter 1:1), Roman provinces in modern Turkey, traditionally in the early 60s AD, before the persecution under Nero.
1 Peter 2: Peter tells believers to "honour the king" (1 Peter 2:17), the emperor, then Nero.
1 Peter 3: Peter addresses wives with unbelieving husbands and believers who suffer for doing good.
1 Peter 4: Peter speaks of a "fiery trial" (1 Peter 4:12) and of suffering "as a Christian" (1 Peter 4:16).
1 Peter 5: Peter writes with Silvanus' help and sends greetings from Mark and the church "at Babylon" (1 Peter 5:12–13), which early Christians understood as Rome.
2 Peter 1: The writer calls himself Simon Peter and expects to die soon (2 Peter 1:14). Tradition places Peter's death in Rome under Nero, about AD 64–67. The letter's authorship was questioned in the early church.
2 Peter 2: The writer warns of false teachers, using examples much like those in Jude.
2 Peter 3: The writer says this is his "second epistle" to the readers (2 Peter 3:1) and refers to Paul's letters.
1 John 1: The letter names no author or place. Tradition links it with the apostle John at Ephesus, late in the 1st century AD.
1 John 2: Some have left the community: "They went out from us" (1 John 2:19).
1 John 3: The writer addresses "little children" about love and righteousness.
1 John 4: "Many false prophets are gone out into the world" (1 John 4:1), denying that Jesus Christ has come in the flesh.
1 John 5: The letter ends with "Little children, keep yourselves from idols" (1 John 5:21).
2 John 1: "The elder" writes to "the elect lady and her children" (2 John 1:1) about traveling teachers. Tradition links it with John at Ephesus late in the 1st century.
3 John 1: "The elder" writes to Gaius about traveling believers and Diotrephes, who refused them hospitality.
Jude 1: Jude, "brother of James" (Jude 1:1), probably the brother of Jesus (Mark 6:3), writes about intruders in the church. The letter gives no date or place; most date it to the second half of the 1st century AD.
Revelation 1: John is on Patmos, an island in the Aegean, and writes to seven churches in the Roman province of Asia (Revelation 1:9, 11). Irenaeus dates it to the end of Domitian's reign, about AD 95; some scholars prefer the late 60s.
Revelation 2: Ephesus, Smyrna, Pergamos, and Thyatira lay on a circular road in western Asia. Pergamos had built the province's first temple to the emperor, in 29 BC.
Revelation 3: Sardis, Philadelphia, and Laodicea lay inland. Sardis and Philadelphia were damaged in the earthquake of AD 17, and Laodicea rebuilt after the earthquake of AD 60 without Roman aid (Tacitus).
Revelation 4: John is called up through a door in heaven and sees God's throne.
Revelation 5: John sees a scroll sealed with seven seals in the right hand of the one on the throne.
Revelation 6: The Lamb opens the first six seals.
Revelation 7: Before the seventh seal, 144,000 from the tribes of Israel are sealed and a great multitude stands before the throne.
Revelation 8: The seventh seal is opened and the first four trumpets sound.
Revelation 9: The fifth and sixth trumpets sound. The river Euphrates (Revelation 9:14) was Rome's eastern frontier with the Parthian empire.
Revelation 10: A mighty angel gives John a little book to eat.
Revelation 11: John is told to measure the temple, and two witnesses prophesy in the city "where also our Lord was crucified" (Revelation 11:8). The seventh trumpet sounds.
Revelation 12: John sees a woman clothed with the sun, a dragon, and war in heaven.
Revelation 13: A beast rises from the sea and another from the earth. Cities in the province of Asia had temples for worship of the emperor.
Revelation 14: The Lamb stands on mount Sion with the 144,000, and three angels announce messages, including "Babylon is fallen" (Revelation 14:8).
Revelation 15: Seven angels with the last seven plagues appear, and the victors sing the song of Moses.
Revelation 16: The seven vials are poured out, and the kings gather at Armageddon (Revelation 16:16), the hill of Megiddo.
Revelation 17: John sees Babylon the great seated on a beast with seven heads, which are "seven mountains" (Revelation 17:9). Rome was known as the city on seven hills.
Revelation 18: Kings, merchants, and sailors mourn Babylon's fall and its lost trade.
Revelation 19: Heaven praises God, the marriage of the Lamb is announced, and a rider called Faithful and True appears.
Revelation 20: Satan is bound for a thousand years, then released; the dead are judged before a great white throne.
Revelation 21: John sees a new heaven and a new earth and the new Jerusalem coming down from God.
Revelation 22: The book ends with the river and tree of life and a warning not to add to or take from its words (Revelation 22:18–19).
